Juvenile recruitment in Jackson Lake springsnail (Pyrgulopsis robusta) begins with the settlement of free-swimming veliger larvae onto suitable substrate, a critical transition that occurs once individuals attain a shell height of 0.11 cm . This species, endemic to the thermal springs of Wyoming, exhibits a life history closely tied to stable water temperatures. Upon hatching from an embryonated egg mass, the planktonic larvae drift for a period before undergoing larval metamorphosis, during which the velum is lost and the juvenile body plan is reorganized. Newly born individuals emerge with a modest shell measuring 0.1 cm [Lb = 0.1 cm], a size that reflects the limited endogenous yolk reserves available to the developing embryo. The post-metamorphic juveniles then begin grazing on epiphytic algae and detritus, initiating a phase of rapid somatic growth. Field surveys indicate that this initial size is consistent across microhabitats, suggesting a canalized developmental pathway during early ontogeny. The transition from a free-swimming to a benthic existence is likely triggered by chemical cues from the substrate, as has been documented in related hydrobiid gastropods. Once settled, the juveniles must contend with intraspecific competition for food resources in the narrow, thermally stable spring runs they inhabit.

As the growing juveniles continue to feed and increase in size, they eventually approach a critical developmental milestone marking the onset of sexual maturation. Puberty in Pyrgulopsis robusta is reached at a shell height of 0.4 cm [Lp = 0.4 cm], a threshold that signifies the commencement of gametogenesis and the development of reproductive organs. This size at maturity is relatively small compared to other members of the Hydrobiidae, consistent with the species' occupation of a stable but resource-limited thermal spring habitat. The shell at this stage demonstrates a clear increase in whorl count and aperture dimensions, reflecting the allometric shift that accompanies the transition from a growing juvenile to a reproductively active adult. Individuals below this size are rarely observed with eggs or developing embryos, confirming that 0.4 cm [Lp = 0.4 cm] represents a reliable indicator of reproductive competence. The timing of this transition is likely mediated by both endogenous physiological cues and exogenous factors such as water temperature and food availability. In the constant thermal environment of Jackson Lake springs, the attainment of this size typically occurs within several months of settlement. This relatively precocious maturation strategy is typical of small-bodied springsnails that experience low predation pressure but face constraints on population density imposed by limited habitable area.

The adult body size of Pyrgulopsis robusta, like its reproductive output, reflects the energetic constraints of its spring-fed habitat. The ultimate shell height attained by fully grown individuals reaches 0.75 cm [Li = 0.75 cm], a dimension that represents the asymptotic size beyond which further somatic growth is negligible. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of a reproductively active adult is 0.137 grams [Wwi = 0.137 grams], a value derived from size-corrected allometric relationships established for Planorbis planorbis and scaled to the shell dimensions of this species. This modest body mass is typical of spring-endemic hydrobiids, which often exhibit reduced adult size compared to their more widespread congeners inhabiting larger lacustrine or riverine systems. The adult shell is elongate-conic in shape, with a relatively high spire and a thickened outer lip that becomes more pronounced in older individuals. The wet weight includes both the soft tissues and the calcareous shell, with the latter constituting a substantial fraction of the total mass. Comparisons with other Pyrgulopsis species indicate that P. robusta falls near the lower end of the size spectrum for the genus, a pattern consistent with its occupation of a geothermally influenced habitat where calcium availability may limit shell deposition. The stable thermal conditions of the springs likely allow for a prolonged period of slow, continuous growth, enabling individuals to approach this asymptotic size reliably.

Longevity in Jackson Lake springsnail has been estimated from mark-recapture studies and life table analyses conducted at a constant temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], yielding a maximum lifespan of 382.0 days [am = 382.0 days]. This duration, just over one full year, places Pyrgulopsis robusta among the shorter-lived members of the Hydrobiidae, a pattern that is consistent with its small body size and relatively high reproductive allocation. Under the controlled laboratory conditions used to derive this estimate, individuals were maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] to match the average water temperature recorded in the spring source during the summer months. The observed lifespan of 382.0 days [am = 382.0 days] suggests an annual semelparous or weakly iteroparous life cycle, wherein most individuals die shortly after completing their reproductive effort in their second calendar year at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. Field observations support this interpretation, as dead, empty shells are most commonly encountered in late summer and early autumn following the peak breeding period. Physiological senescence in this species is likely accelerated by the energetic demands of gamete production, which imposes a significant metabolic cost on the relatively small adult body. The close coupling of lifespan with water temperature also implies that even minor shifts in the thermal regime of the springs could have disproportionate effects on population persistence by compressing the window available for growth and reproduction.
